mink.origin: Farmed mink is the American mink, Neogale vison (formerly Neovison vison or Mustela vison), a semi-aquatic mustelid native to North America that is bred in cages for its pelt. In 2020 Denmark had about 1,100 mink farms, and more than 15 million mink were culled there late that year. Selective breeding has produced color types such as Nordic Brown and American Black, and Danish researchers have tested genomic selection for size and fur traits. Mink enters textiles as dressed pelts and trim, not as spun fiber.
mink.structure: A mink pelt is skin carrying two hair populations: long, stiff guard hairs and a dense underfur, called wool in mink grading, that provides insulation. Graders score guard hair length, guard hair thickness, underfur density, silky appearance and overall quality; these traits show low to moderate heritability, with quantitative trait loci mapped on several chromosomes. Selection for underfur density improved guard hair quality and almost eliminated the defect called metallic sheen. The hairs are keratin, with medullated guard hairs, and the skin is a collagen network that must be stabilized by dressing.
mink.process: The winter coat grows during the growing-furring period, from about mid-September until pelting in December. Diet matters: cutting dietary protein reduced the number and diameter of under hairs and guard hairs and shortened pelts, and anemia in young kits leads to the cotton fur defect. Animals are graded alive, killed and pelted, and the dried skins are graded again and sold. Pelts are then dressed, a tanning process that stabilizes the skin while retaining the hair, before being matched and sewn into garments or trim.
mink.performance: Fur insulates by trapping still air in the dense underfur, while guard hairs shed water and protect the underfur from abrasion. Guard hairs break and underfur mats with wear, and the dressed skin is sensitive to heat, water and solvents, which is why specialist cleaning is advised. In a laboratory study, SARS-CoV-2 remained infectious for up to 10 days on mink fur, longer than on cotton or faux fur; UV light failed to inactivate it on pelts, whereas heating at 60 C for one hour inactivated it on all tested surfaces.
mink.identify: Burn tests on a few hairs (indicative only, and to be done with care) show keratin behavior, whereas acrylic or modacrylic faux fur melts; checking for a skin rather than a knitted or woven backing at the hair base is a simpler non-destructive clue. Species identification uses guard hair microscopy (scale pattern, medulla and cross-section) against reference hairs, or DNA analysis. Dyeing and shearing can disguise species, so pelts should be matched to documentation.
mink.labeling: In the US, fur apparel falls under the Fur Products Labeling Act, whose FTC rules at 16 CFR Part 301 govern how the animal name and other information appear on labels, invoices and advertising. In the EU, Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 requires textile products that contain non-textile parts of animal origin, such as fur trim, to state this on the label. After SARS-CoV-2 reached farmed mink, entire national mink populations were culled and production banned in some countries; Denmark enacted an interim ban on mink production until the end of 2021 after culling its entire herd in 2020.
mink.past: Fur farming as a whole began in the mid-nineteenth century. The modern turning point was SARS-CoV-2: infection in farmed mink was detected in the Netherlands in April 2020 and in Denmark in June, where 290 farms became infected, mink-associated variants including the Cluster 5 lineage spread to an estimated 4,000 people, and the government culled the entire population of more than 15 million mink. In 2025 a European Food Safety Authority opinion concluded that key welfare consequences of current cage systems, including restricted movement and inability to explore or forage, could not be prevented or substantially mitigated within those systems.

fox.origin: Farmed fox fur comes mainly from two species: the red fox, Vulpes vulpes, farmed in color types sold as silver fox, and the Arctic fox, Vulpes lagopus, known in the trade as blue fox. Arctic foxes have been farmed intensively since the early 1900s, and genomic work traces all Fennoscandian farmed Arctic foxes to a coastal ecotype related to the wild Icelandic population. Recent veterinary literature also describes extensive fox farming in China, including farms in Shandong, Hebei and Liaoning provinces.
fox.structure: Fox pelts have long, fine guard hairs over a dense, woolly underfur, giving the high, soft pile used for collars and trim. The hairs are keratin: guard hairs have a cuticle, cortex and medulla, while underfur hairs are finer and wavier. Farming has selected for color phases, body size and fur traits, and farmed Arctic foxes show reduced genome-wide heterozygosity and long runs of homozygosity compared with wild populations, signs of inbreeding during incipient domestication. The skin is a collagen network that must be dressed to become a stable leather.
fox.process: Farmed foxes grow their winter coat during an autumn fur-growing period, when dietary protein and amino acids such as methionine influence growth and fur quality. After killing and pelting, skins are dried, graded and sold, then dressed and in many cases dyed or sheared before being cut and sewn, often as trims and collars. Dense husbandry also carries disease risks: in 2023, severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus caused outbreaks lasting two to three months on six Arctic fox farms in Shandong and Liaoning provinces.
fox.performance: The long guard hair and dense underfur trap air, giving strong insulation and a lofty look, but long hairs break, tangle and mat under friction, as at collar edges. Dressed skins can stiffen or shrink if wetted and heated, so cleaning should be left to fur specialists. Like other keratin, the hair is attacked by clothes moth and carpet beetle larvae, and pelts need cool, ventilated storage. In laboratory tests on pelts including blue fox, UV light failed to inactivate SARS-CoV-2, while heating at 60 C for one hour did.
fox.identify: Burn tests (indicative only, and to be done with care) show keratin behavior, while acrylic or modacrylic faux fur melts; a knitted or woven backing marks faux fur and a skin backing marks real fur. Species identification relies on guard hair microscopy against reference hairs or on DNA, because dyeing and shearing can obscure species differences. Microsatellite markers developed for the Chinese raccoon dog also amplify in Arctic and silver foxes, one example of genetic tools usable for identification.
fox.labeling: In the US, fur apparel falls under the Fur Products Labeling Act, whose FTC rules at 16 CFR Part 301 govern how the animal name and other information appear on labels, invoices and advertising. In the EU, Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 requires textile products that contain non-textile parts of animal origin, such as fur trim, to state this on the label. Trade names such as silver fox and blue fox describe farmed color types of two different species; they do not replace the species identification that labels and documentation should support.
fox.past: Fur farming began in the mid-nineteenth century, and Arctic foxes have been bred intensively since the early 1900s, producing incipient domestication with inbreeding and loss of genetic variation. Research on farmed foxes now spans nutrition, reproduction and welfare, including validated fecal cortisol measures and trials of shelter screens that interact with individual personality. In 2025 a European Food Safety Authority opinion identified restricted movement, inability to explore or forage and sensory under- or overstimulation as major welfare consequences of current cages, with species-specific handling stress, locomotory disorders in Arctic foxes and group stress in red foxes.
facts: Vulpes vulpes (silver fox and other color types); Vulpes lagopus (blue fox)
reduced heterozygosity and long runs of homozygosity
